displayQuote: Those who play with the devil's toys will be brought by degrees to wield his sword

meta.title: Who really said "Those who play with the devil's toys will be brought by degrees to wield his sword"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Buckminster Fuller. Thomas Fuller wrote it in 1642 — and he wrote "devil's rattles," not "toys." The primary source, verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Those who play with the devil's toys will be brought by degrees to wield his sword'?
meta.ogDescription: A surname mix-up moved this line from a 1642 witch-sketch to a 20th-century futurist. The real source, and the word that got swapped.

answer.label: Not Buckminster Fuller — actually Thomas Fuller
answer.sourceLine: Thomas Fuller — the seventeenth-century English clergyman, not the twentieth-century American designer — wrote the line in The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), in his character sketch of “The Witch.” His words were “the devils rattles,” not “the devil’s toys”; Quote Investigator ↗ found no evidence that Buckminster Fuller ever said or wrote any version of it.

source.heading: The 1642 passage

docMeta.dd: The Holy State and the Profane State
The Fifth Book, chapter 3: “The Witch,” p. 367
1642 — Cambridge, printed by Roger Daniel for John Williams
“devil’s toys” — a later alteration of Fuller’s “devils rattles,” origin undocumented

source.excerpt: She begins at first with doing tricks rather strange then hurtfull: yea some of them are pretty and pleasing. But it is dangerous to gather floures that grow on the banks of the pit of hell, for fear of falling in; yea they which play with the devils rattles, will be brought by degrees to wield his sword, and from making of sport they come to doing of mischief.
source.trailTitle: How “rattles” became “toys,” and Thomas became Buckminster
trail: 1642 — Thomas Fuller publishes The Holy State and the Profane State in Cambridge. In the sketch “The Witch” he writes that those who play with the devil’s rattles will by degrees wield his sword, per Quote Investigator’s transcription of the first edition ↗.
1840 — William Pickering’s London edition carries the passage in modernised spelling on p. 295, still with rattles. We read it in the Internet Archive scan ↗.

1902 and 1921 — the line circulates detached from its book: Chamber’s Cyclopaedia of English Literature lists it among Fuller’s “pithy shorter sayings,” and The Evening World of New York prints it with the bare tag “—Fuller,” both documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

2005 and 2010 — the Buckminster credit surfaces in print: a letter in Oregon’s Register-Guard asks whether “Buckminster Fuller” was warning about devil’s toys, and a compilation lists the line as “R. Buckminster Fuller, 1895” — 1895 being his birth year, not a date of writing. Both citations are from Quote Investigator ↗.
source.cutTag: The Profane State (1642), Book V, ch. 3 — “The Witch”
source.excerptNote: As transcribed from the 1642 first edition by Quote Investigator ↗; “floures” is an old spelling of flowers, and the original prints “devils” without an apostrophe. The 1840 Pickering edition ↗ modernises it to “they who play with the devil’s rattles.” One curiosity, offered as an observation rather than an explanation: the word toys does appear in Fuller’s very next paragraph in that edition — “He is to find her some toys for a time” — but no source links that to the modern swap.

source.rightsNote: Thomas Fuller’s The Holy State and the Profane State was first published in 1642 and its author died in 1661, so the text quoted here is long in the public domain worldwide; the 1840 Pickering edition we read it in is likewise free of copyright. Note that this status attaches to Fuller’s actual sentence — the popular “devil’s toys” rewording has no identifiable author or first printing at all, which is a reason to quote Fuller’s wording rather than the internet’s.

author.name: Thomas Fuller
author.heading: The Fuller who actually wrote it
author.bio: Thomas Fuller was an English clergyman and historian, baptised in June 1608 and dead in August 1661 — and, as Wikipedia puts it, one of the first English writers able to live by his pen. His best-loved book, The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), is a gallery of short character sketches — the good widow, the good servant, the witch — written in a compressed, epigrammatic style that throws off aphorisms almost by accident. That style is exactly why his sentences travel so well without him: they sound like proverbs, and proverbs lose their authors.

copyAttribution: "Those who play with the devil's toys will be brought by degrees to wield his sword." — NOT Buckminster Fuller. Thomas Fuller (1608–1661) wrote "they which play with the devils rattles, will be brought by degrees to wield his sword" in The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), Fifth Book, ch. 3, "The Witch," p. 367. The "devil's toys" wording is a later, unsourced alteration; Quote Investigator found no evidence Buckminster Fuller ever used the line. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Two things went wrong here
misattribution.intro: This is a double error: the wrong Fuller, and the wrong word. Both are worth separating, because correcting only the name still leaves you quoting a sentence Thomas Fuller did not write.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports it “has located no substantive evidence that Buckminster Fuller employed the words” and concludes the modern ascription was mistaken. The line does not appear anywhere on his Wikiquote page ↗ either.

The saying circulated for decades credited only to the surname — Quote Investigator ↗ shows The Evening World printing it in 1921 as simply “—Fuller,” and suggests someone later misread that ambiguous tag and reassigned the words from Thomas to Buckminster.
Fuller wrote rattles. The 1840 edition ↗ reads “they who play with the devil’s rattles will be brought by degrees to wield his sword.” No source documents who changed rattles to toys, or when.
AZQuotes ↗ still files the “devil’s toys” wording under R. Buckminster Fuller, with no source and no note.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Thomas Fuller’s, from 1642. The famous wording is nobody’s — an anonymous later edit — and the famous author never touched it. See Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why a witch-sketch line reads like a warning about technology
lead: Fuller was not writing about gadgets. The sentence sits in a character sketch of the witch, describing a woman who starts out doing parlour tricks — charms and spells that are, in his phrase, “pretty and pleasing” — and slides from harmless mischief into real harm. The whole passage is an escalation argument: the danger is not the first small step, it is the gradient.

That shape is why the line survived its own context. Strip out the witch and it becomes a general law about dabbling — which is precisely how a modern reader hears it, and precisely why it feels like something a systems thinker and futurist might have said about the atom bomb or the machine age. The fit is the trap: it is so plausible as Buckminster Fuller that nobody checked.
context.detailsSummary: What Fuller actually argued in “The Witch”
detailsBody: Fuller’s sketch runs as a sequence: the witch begins defensively, with charms meant to protect her against the plots of enemies; she moves to tricks that are strange rather than hurtful; and only then does she, in his words, indent downright with the devil. The famous sentence is the hinge in that sequence — the moment where play becomes power.

The compressed, proverb-like phrasing is characteristic of the whole book. The Holy State and the Profane State sold out its first printing and was reprinted repeatedly, which is one reason individual sentences from it circulated for centuries with no more attribution than the bare surname “Fuller.”
context.pull: The danger is not the first small step. It is the gradient.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Buckminster Fuller used the words, attributes the saying to Thomas Fuller's The Profane State (1642), Fifth Book ch. 3 'The Witch', p. 367 (Cambridge, Roger Daniel for John Williams), transcribes the 1642 passage including 'floures' and 'devils rattles', and documents the 1902 Chamber's Cyclopaedia, 1921 Evening World ('—Fuller'), 2005 Register-Guard and 2010 'Iron Sharpens Iron' (R. Buckminster Fuller, 1895) citations.

The full text of the 1840 William Pickering edition contains, on p. 295 in 'The Witch': 'they who play with the devil's rattles will be brought by degrees to wield his sword, and from making of sport they come to doing of mischief', preceded by the 'flowers... banks of the pit of hell' sentence and followed by 'He is to find her some toys for a time'. Archive metadata gives publisher London: William Pickering, year 1840, creator Fuller, Thomas, 1608-1661.

Wikiquote's Thomas Fuller page carries '[T]hey which play with the devils rattles, will be brought by degrees to wield his sword[.]' sourced to The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), 'The Witch', and gives Fuller's dates as baptised 19 June 1608 – died 16 August 1661, English preacher, historian and scholar.
Wikiquote's Buckminster Fuller page does not contain 'devil's toys', 'devil's rattles' or 'wield his sword' in any section, including Misattributed.

Thomas Fuller was baptised 19 June 1608 and died 16 August 1661; he was an English clergyman and historian, 'a prolific author, and one of the first English writers able to live by his pen'; The Holy State and the Profane State was published in 1642 and was perhaps the most popular of his writings.

The Holy State and the Profane State is a 1642 book by Thomas Fuller comprising four books of character archetypes and profane biographies; its first print run sold out and it was reprinted four times.
R. Buckminster Fuller was born 12 July 1895 and died 1 July 1983; he was an American architect, systems theorist, writer, designer, inventor, philosopher and futurist.
AZQuotes attributes 'Those who play with the devil's toys will be brought by degrees to wield his sword.' to R. Buckminster Fuller with no source cited.
